items.title: Iran war pushes African, South Asian homes back to charcoal and firewood

featured_image.name: African woman cooking over an open fire in Nigeria, Africa

items.description:
Before sunset in Nairobi's Kibera settlement, Brenda Obare used to cook dinner with a quick turn of her gas stove's knob. Now she crouches over a charcoal burner, coaxing a smoky fire outside her tin-roofed home. "We don't have many options," she told the Associated Press. "You use what you can afford."[1]

Obare's story has become emblematic of a cascading crisis. The war between the United States, Israel, and Iran — which began in late February and led to the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz — has disrupted roughly 20 percent of global oil and liquefied natural gas trade. As energy prices surged more than 55 percent since the conflict began, the shockwaves have reached the kitchens, forests, and wildlife habitats of Africa and South Asia, threatening years of progress in public health and conservation.[2][3][1]

items.description: World military expenditure reached $2.887 trillion in 2025, marking the 11th consecutive annual increase and the highest level ever recorded, according to new data released Monday by the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (SIPRI). The 2.9 percent real-terms increase pushed global military spending to 2.5 percent of GDP, its highest share since 2009.[1][2][3]

items.title: Zelenskyy says EU accession talks could open in June

featured_image.name: Ukraine officially begins EU accession negotiations

items.description:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Sunday that he expects the European Union to formally open the first negotiating clusters for Ukraine's accession talks as soon as June, declaring that Kyiv has fulfilled all the preparatory requirements demanded by Brussels.

"We see approximate dates, maybe in June," Zelenskyy said, according to Liga.net, adding that a decision on the clusters could come between late May and June. The remarks came after a meeting in Kyiv with Moldovan President Maia Sandu, with both leaders pressing the EU to move forward on membership negotiations without further delay.[1][2]

items.title: China quietly expands economic pressure toolkit during trade truce

featured_image.name: Chips and clouds: U.S.-China trade war escalates

items.description:
Even as Washington and Beijing publicly prepare for a mid-May summit between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, China has been quietly assembling a broad new arsenal of economic countermeasures under cover of the trade truce the two leaders struck last October in Busan, South Korea.

Since that meeting — which Trump rated "a 12 out of 10" — Beijing has enacted sweeping new laws, tightened export controls on critical minerals, banned foreign AI chips from state-funded data centers, barred American and Israeli cybersecurity software from Chinese firms, and begun weighing restrictions on solar manufacturing equipment exports to the United States, according to a Reuters analysis published on Sunday.[1][2]

items.title: Chile's dark skies remain at risk despite energy project cancellation, scientists warn

featured_image.name: Light pollution is threatening the darkest skies on Earth. Here's how ...

items.description:
In one of the driest and darkest places on Earth, astronomers have secured a hard-fought victory to preserve the night sky — but they warn the fight is far from over.

AES Andes, a subsidiary of the U.S. energy company AES Corporation, formally withdrew its proposed INNA green energy project from Chile's Environmental Assessment Service in February, ending a yearlong confrontation between the scientific community and a sprawling industrial development planned just 10 kilometers from the European Southern Observatory's Paranal Observatory in the Atacama Desert.[1][2]
